units: a newly learnt idea leaves at first an unsteady mental trace
that trace is made firm above all during sleep
networks of neurons replay the acquired sequence during that phase
going over the material too soon after learning brings almost no gain
a slight forgetting before the review increases its effect
recalling without help fixes the material better than reading it again
specialists advise widening the gap between two reviews step by step
writing the idea down and then trying to say it back from memory produces lasting knowledge
text: Understanding an idea in class is not the end of learning it. What the brain lays down at first is a faint trace, and a faint trace rubs out easily. The work that makes it hold comes later, above all while we sleep: networks of neurons run the newly acquired sequence again and again until it settles. Go over the material straight away and you gain almost nothing, because none of it has faded yet. Wait until it has begun to slip, and the mind must rebuild what it lost, and that effort of recall fixes far more than another read-through ever will. This is why specialists on learning tell you to stretch the gap between reviews, a little wider each time. Write the idea on a card, put the card away, then try to say the whole thing back without looking: what you keep that way, you keep.

units: a bookbinding workshop came close to shutting down
its last craftsman lost the use of one of his hands
the movements of the trade had never been written down
the manager had the craftsman recorded while he described each operation
an apprentice carried out the movements while he corrected her aloud
out of it came a manual naming the commonest fault at every stage
the workshop carried on and drew applicants from far away
the injury of one man set off the writing down of a practice until then spoken
text: A bookbinding workshop came within days of shutting when its last craftsman lost the use of one hand. Nothing of the trade had ever been set down on paper; the whole of it lived in the fingers of that one man, and the manager knew it would go with him. So she had him recorded while he talked his way through every operation, from sewing the sections to gluing the spine, laying the headbands and paring the leather. An apprentice did the work with her own hands, and he watched and corrected her aloud. Out of that came a manual nobody had planned, one that named, at each stage, the mistake most people make. The workshop stayed open, and word of the manual drew applicants from far away. An injury to a single pair of hands had put a wholly spoken craft into writing for the first time.

units: the words are missing at the moment of giving back what has been noted
the method offered rests on a notebook kept for that purpose alone
every page is divided into two columns of unequal width
the wide column takes the word as it was met and a whole sentence holding it
the narrow column takes a definition worded by the learner himself
a mark is added each week the word still slips away
words gathering too many marks are copied out apart and gone over aloud
at the end of a season the notebook forms a word list belonging to its own author
text: Your notes pile up and nothing sticks to them: the moment you have to say it back, the words are not there. The remedy is a slim notebook kept for that purpose alone. Rule every page into two columns of unequal width. In the wide one, put down the word as you met it, along with a whole sentence that carries it. In the narrow one, write a definition in your own wording, never lifted from somewhere else. Each week the word still slips away from you, add a small mark beside it. Once a word has gathered too many marks, copy it out on its own sheet, then stand up and go through that sheet aloud with the definition hidden. By the end of a season the notebook has turned into a word list that belongs to nobody but you, and every entry in it carries the trace of what it cost you.

units: two local workshops announce the same aim of mending things oneself
the first workshop is run as a lecture from the front
those attending the first leave with papers they will never open again
the second workshop is built around the machines brought in by those who come
there one gets on by sitting beside someone who has already taken a similar machine apart
the organisers of the second admit that their way of doing it is muddled and noisy
those attending the second come back while those of the first grow fewer
the gap between the two workshops comes from where the question starts
text: Two neighbourhood workshops make exactly the same promise: teaching ordinary people to mend their own broken things. The first one runs like a lecture. A trainer talks from the front, holds up the tools, hands round a printed booklet, and everybody goes home with a wad of paper they will never open again. The second runs on whatever people carry through the door. You sit beside someone who has already had the back off a machine like yours, and you get on by following your own fault to the end of it. The pair who run the second are the first to call their way of doing it noisy, muddled and impossible to grade. Yet their lot turn up again the week after, while the lecture crowd thins out by the third evening. The difference is not in the kit on the table. It is in who asks the question.

units: a smell of white dust takes hold as soon as one enters the room
a worn raised platform carries a narrow table and a chair that does not match
a dark board runs the whole width of the wall and keeps strokes that will not rub out
the rows of school desks each keep a hollow groove now left unused
notches were cut into the wood by impatient hands
boxes of yellowed writings are piled along the ledge of the openings
a glazed cupboard holds rolled maps a skeleton and jars
the room now serves as a store although nothing has been taken out of it
text: Push the door and the chalk dust catches you at once, dry and faintly damp at the same time. At the far end, a low wooden platform worn hollow by boot leather carries a narrow table and a chair that never matched it. A black board runs the whole width of the wall, scored with pale strokes that no cloth will lift now. The desks stand in rows, each keeping its groove for the ink well, long dry, and its notches cut into the wood by hands with nothing better to do. Along the window ledge sit boxes of yellowed exercise papers covered in a careful hand. A glazed cupboard holds rolled maps, a wooden skeleton and dusty jars whose labels are peeling off. Nothing was thrown out and nothing replaced: the room is a store now, and you walk into it as into a memory left standing open.

units: the ease of deleting a word harms the teaching of writing
the pupil of former times left the mark of his waverings on the page
the rough draft was held to be the proof of a path of thought
the coming of electronic supports made correction invisible
a deleted mistake can no longer be read again by the one who made it
one gets better by going back over what one missed and not by handing in a clean page
the teacher deprived of the rough draft judges only an outcome
the writer argues for giving the marks of correction their standing back
text: Deleting has become too easy, and the teaching of writing loses more by it than we care to admit. A pupil once wrote in ink, and the page held on to every wavering: a crossing-out, a word called back into the margin, a sentence begun again two lines lower. The rough draft was no waste paper. It was the proof that a mind had travelled. Then came the screens, where a correction leaves no scar at all. The pupil deletes, the error evaporates, and with it goes any chance of reading that error again. Yet nobody learns by handing in a clean page. We learn by going back over what we got wrong. A teacher shown only the finished version has no sight of the thinking; a destination is marked and the journey lost. Give the crossing-out its standing back, and error becomes a tool once more.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman teaching at the workshop earlier worked as a potter
a condition of the joints forced her to give up the wheel
that injury is the reason she moved to teaching
she can no longer show a movement over a long stretch of time
she therefore cut every movement into short steps named with precision
her pupils receive words that other workshops leave unspoken
her apprentices get on faster than those trained by copying alone
being able to describe a fault before putting it right explains that lead
text: The woman who teaches at the pottery workshop spent most of her working life at the wheel herself. Inflamed joints in both wrists took that away from her, and it is the injury, not a calling, that put her in front of a class. Since she can no longer keep her hands on the clay for a whole session to show how it is done, she had to break the work into short steps and give each one an exact name: centring, opening, raising the wall, smoothing. Her pupils come away with words that most workshops never bother to say out loud, because there the thing is simply copied. That has had an effect nobody foresaw. Her apprentices move ahead faster than those taught by copying, since they can put a fault into words before they put it right. One woman's damaged wrists changed how a whole trade is taught.

units: the book of exercises is addressed to apprentice carpenters
its material making and its pictures are held to be of good quality
the rising order of the difficulties looks carefully thought out
the work shows only movements that came out right and never ones that went wrong
a learner who gets it wrong finds no page describing his fault
that absence leads the learner to lay the blame for failure on himself alone
the writer of the review suggests adding facing it the picture of the spoiled piece
he also suggests joining to that picture the question to ask oneself before it
text: The book of exercises written for apprentice carpenters has a flaw that no amount of good making can redeem. The binding is sound, the drawings are clean, and the ladder of difficulty has clearly been thought about at length. Where it fails is on one decisive point: it shows the cut that came out right, and never the cut that came out wrong. An apprentice who saws off the line finds no page telling him what a fault looks like, or what it does to the joint once assembled. He tends to conclude that the failure lies in him alone. Putting this right would cost little. Facing each plate, the makers need only set a picture of the spoiled piece, and beside that picture the question to ask when you are standing over it. That one addition would turn a handsome object into a teaching tool.

units: the reader is torn between evening lessons and going straight into apprenticeship
the writer of the letter has followed both of these paths
the evening teaching announces its programme and marks the exercises
on that path a failure costs no more than a harsh comment
the workshop announces nothing and one learns there by starting again after getting it wrong
a mistake made in the workshop is paid for in spoiled material
the writer advises beginning with the evening lessons
he recommends noting down what one fails to understand in a notebook before turning up at the workshop
craftsmen willingly take in a newcomer who brings precise questions
text: You ask me whether to take the evening lessons or go straight into the workshop as an apprentice. I have done both, and what separates them has stayed with me. The lessons come in order: you are told what will be covered, your exercises come back marked, and failing costs you nothing worse than a harsh comment on the page. The workshop tells you nothing in advance. You watch, you get it wrong, you begin again, and getting it wrong there is paid for in ruined material. What you gain is a steadiness that no lesson hands over. My advice is short. Start with the lessons, keep a small notebook of everything you fail to understand, then turn up at the workshop with those pages in your pocket. The trade takes kindly to anyone who arrives with a precise question. Write and tell me what you choose.

units: the question asked bears on what parts a trainer who marks people from one soon forgotten
the woman running a retraining centre puts the difference down to patience with being asked the same thing again
she names first the listening that lets the learner finish his mistaken sentence
she names next the cutting of the task into portions small enough to keep failure away
she names the bad example where the trainer performs the wrong movement himself before everyone
she names last the silence kept while the learner is working the answer out
the poor trainer talks too much and moves on too fast
he takes the neatness of his own account for understanding among those listening
she holds that one becomes a trainer by watching others get it wrong
text: So what makes one trainer stay with you for years while another goes clean out of your head? The woman who runs a retraining centre answers without pausing: patience with being asked the same thing again. Then she breaks it down. Listening comes first, since a good trainer lets you finish the wrong sentence instead of cutting across it. Then the slicing: the task is cut into pieces so small that failing at one is hard. Then the bad example, where she makes the wrong move herself, in front of the room, and owns it. Last of all, silence, because she keeps quiet while the learner is getting there. And the poor trainer? Talks too much, pushes on too fast, and takes the neatness of his own account for understanding in the room. Nobody, she adds, becomes a trainer by reciting. You become one by watching people get it wrong.
